title: First Unique Character in a String
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning per character versus counting once then scanning again.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, return the index of the first character that does not repeat anywhere else in the string. If no such character exists, return -1.

blocks.text: Given a string s, return the index of the first character that does not repeat anywhere else in the string. If no such character exists, return -1.

blocks.title: Analogy: The First Guest Who Only Signed In Once
blocks.text: Like checking a guest book for the first name that appears only a single time, even though many other names in the book might show up two or three times each.

blocks.caption: Find the first character position whose letter appears nowhere else in the string

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["l appears once, and it is the first character","no earlier character to check","the very first position already satisfies the uniqueness requirement"],["Answer","0","l never repeats anywhere else in the string"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["l and o both repeat later in the string","v at index 2 is the first character that never repeats","l appears again at index 4, o appears again at index 9, but v appears only once in the whole string"],["Answer","2","v is the first index whose character has a total count of exactly 1"]]}

blocks.text: Every character in this string appears at least twice, so there is no unique character at all, giving -1.
It helps to ask exactly when a character's true, final count actually becomes knowable.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Valid Anagram already showed that tallying every character once, with a hash map, replaces rescanning the string repeatedly to learn how many times each value occurs.

Observation 2: Applying that same tally directly here would let every position's count be looked up instantly, but the count for the very first character can only be trusted once the entire string has actually been scanned, since a character seen early might still repeat much later.

Observation 3: This means, unlike some counting problems, a single forward pass genuinely cannot answer the question, the count must be finished completely before the search for "the first index with count 1" can even begin.

Observation 4: Doing exactly that, count every character once across the whole string, then walk the string again in its original left to right order checking each character's now-known count, correctly finds the answer, confirmed by tracing s equal to "loveleetcode" through to the correct index, 2.

Recognizing that a character's true count is only knowable after the whole string is read is what makes this a genuine two pass problem, count first, then search in order, rather than something solvable in a single pass.
For every character in the string, scan the entire string again to count how many times that character appears, and return the first position whose count is exactly 1.

items: For every index i, count how many times s[i] appears anywhere in the whole string.
If that count is exactly 1, return i immediately.
If no such index is found, return -1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every position independently rescans the entire string to compute its own character's count, so no counting work is shared between positions.
The first index found with a count of exactly 1 is returned immediately, since positions are checked in their natural left to right order already.
Returning -1 after the full loop correctly signals that no unique character exists anywhere in the string.

blocks.text: Every character's true total count is directly computed, so the first genuinely unique character is correctly identified.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), rescanning the whole string for every position.
Space: O(1) extra, no additional structure is used.
Limitation: the same counts get recomputed from scratch for every single position, when every character's total count could instead be computed once, up front.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: the same character's count is recomputed by a full rescan every single time it is encountered as a candidate, even though its true count never changes.

What counting once up front fixes: a single pass with a hash map or fixed size array tallies every character's total frequency exactly once, for the entire string, regardless of how many positions share that character.

Why one pass alone still is not enough: the first position's count cannot be trusted until every later occurrence of that same character has also been seen, so the counting pass must fully finish before any position can be judged.

The core idea: count completely in one pass first, then make a second pass in the original order, now safely using each character's finished count to find the very first one equal to 1.

Count every character's total frequency across the whole string in a single pass, using a hash map or a fixed size array for the alphabet. Then walk through the string a second time, in its original order, and return the first index whose character has a count of exactly 1.
Count every character once, then scan again to find the first one with a count of exactly 1.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Count every letter","l:2, o:2, v:1, e:4, t:1, c:1, d:1"],["Scan in order: l (count 2), o (count 2), v (count 1)","v is the first with count exactly 1"],["Answer","index 2"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: count every character once, then scan in order for the first count of 1

blocks.text: This works because the counting pass finishes before the search pass begins, so every count consulted during the second scan is already the character's true, final total, guaranteeing that the first index found with a count of exactly 1 truly never repeats anywhere else in the string.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A character's finished count is greater than 1","The second scan simply skips past that position","Repeating characters are correctly passed over, in original left to right order"],["A character's finished count equals exactly 1","That index is returned immediately during the second scan","The first, leftmost genuinely unique character is correctly identified"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear passes.
Space: O(1), since the alphabet size is fixed.

blocks.text: This is another instance of the "count once, then scan again in original order" pattern, useful whenever a question depends on both a value's frequency and its position.

items: Trying to determine uniqueness during a single forward pass, which is not possible since a character's full count cannot be known until the whole string has been seen.
Returning the character itself instead of its index, which is what the problem actually asks for.

blocks.text: Point out explicitly why one pass alone cannot work: a character seen early might still repeat later, so its final count is only known once the whole string has been scanned.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this in one pass", think: explain clearly why counting genuinely requires seeing the whole string first, then the search is a necessary second pass.
If the interviewer says "what if the input were streamed and could not be revisited", think: an ordered structure like a queue of candidates, removing entries as they are proven to repeat, is the standard streaming adaptation.
If the interviewer says "what about non lowercase-letter alphabets", think: swap the fixed size array for a hash map, the two pass logic stays identical.

items: Why can this problem not be solved correctly in a single forward pass?
How would you adapt this approach if s could contain any Unicode character, not just lowercase English letters?
How would you solve this if the string arrived as a live stream of characters that could not be revisited?
How would you find the k-th unique character instead of just the first one?
How would you adapt this to find the first character that repeats exactly twice, rather than exactly once?
Valid Anagram, whose single pass counting is the direct ancestor of tallying characters here, though that problem never needed a second pass since it only checks totals, not positions.
Longest Common Prefix, whose single running candidate replaced repeated pairwise comparison, a related "avoid recomputation" instinct applied differently here.
Any problem needing both a value's total frequency and its earliest position, where a count-first, search-second two pass structure is the standard, reliable approach.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: count every character once in a first pass, then scan again in original order to find the first count of exactly 1.
Core Idea: a character's true count is only knowable after the entire string has been read, so counting must fully finish before the search for the first unique character can begin.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) for both approaches.

Most Important Observation: this problem genuinely requires two passes, one to establish complete counts, one to search in original order, since no single pass could know a character's final count in advance.
Interview Difficulty: the two pass idea is simple and standard; clearly explaining why a single pass cannot work is the detail that shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: count everything first, only then can you trust any single count while scanning in order.
